source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
EdgeCore Ashburn AS01 publishes 114 MW of IT capacity, the third largest figure among Virginia data centers that disclose one, and nothing about the power behind it.

Disclosure is the exception in Virginia, not the rule. Twenty five of the state's 330 mapped facilities publish a megawatt figure, and those 25 total 1,603 MW, of which this Sterling campus is 7.1 percent. Its 114 MW sits across 685,000 square feet of technical space, which at 40 kW per rack implies roughly 2,850 racks, though the operator does not state workload mix or actual tenant configuration.

That arithmetic is the only bridge this record offers between a building and AI compute. Rack count follows from capacity and density, and capacity is the input that training clusters consume. But the number that determines whether the campus can actually run is the one absent from the filing: whether its power comes from existing utility supply or new generation, and where it connects to the grid. LEED certification speaks to efficiency standards, not to power source or grid characteristics.

The record also cannot say whether the full 114 MW is allocated or available, or who occupies it. A facility can rank third in published capacity and still be unassessable as a contributor to Virginia's AI scaling constraint, because published capacity measures what a building was designed to hold, not what the grid has agreed to deliver.
